The core insight is that a spinor picks up a sign under a 2π rotation and needs a full 4π (720°) to return to its original state. It fits better than most product names do, and the 720° detail is exactly the load-bearing part.

**The double cover is the shape of your write path.** A spinor lives in a representation of Spin(n), the double cover of the rotation group. Rotate it by 2π and it doesn't come back — it comes back as *minus itself*. Only the second full turn restores it. The reason is topological: SO(3) has fundamental group ℤ/2, so a 360° loop in rotation space is not contractible, while the 720° loop is. Spinors are the objects that can tell the difference.

That's structurally the same statement as the core decision in the data layer I just ported. A source does not become a fact in one step. Extraction gets you to something that *looks* like knowledge and sits in exactly the right place — same entity, same claim, same anchors — but carries the opposite sign. It's a proposal. The second rotation, human confirmation through `resolveProposalItems`, is what returns it to identity. A system that treated one turn as sufficient is an LLM writing straight into a database. Naming the product after the class of object for which one turn is provably not enough is a fairly precise piece of self-description.

**Path-dependence is the other half.** A spinor's state depends on the route taken, not just the endpoint. Two spinors at the same orientation can differ by sign because one got there the long way. Your fact model does this deliberately: `supersededBy` and `validUntil` mean the currently-valid set carries its own derivation. Two knowledge bases with identical current facts are *not* the same knowledge base if one arrived by supersession and the other by assertion. A company brain that stored only current state would be storing vectors. You're storing spinors.

**And the sign only matters relationally** — which is the subtle part, and the part that saves the metaphor from being decorative. The overall sign of a single isolated spinor is unobservable. What's observable is the *relative* sign between two of them. This isn't hand-waving: Rauch and Werner independently measured it in 1975 by splitting a neutron beam, rotating one arm through 2π, and watching the interference pattern invert. Same in your system. No single fact's provenance matters much on its own. The moment two accounts of the same engagement disagree, `confirmedBy` and the retained proposal trail stop being overhead and become the entire answer. That's why proposals survive resolution instead of being deleted — the extra structure can't be reconstructed from the observables, exactly as spinors can't be built from SO(3) alone.

There's a nice practical bonus: every graphics programmer has already handled a spinor without calling it that. Unit quaternions are the concrete model, and everyone who's written rotation code knows *q* and *−q* give the same rotation. And for non-technical explanation you get the belt trick — hand someone a belt, put one twist in it, watch them fail to remove it without releasing the ends, then add a second twist and watch it fall out. Having a physical demo of your product thesis is not nothing.

**Where I'd stop pushing it.** The honest seam is that for a single isolated spinor, the 2π state is *physically indistinguishable* from the 0 state — the sign is gauge in isolation. Pushed too hard, the metaphor implies the review step changes nothing observable, which inverts your thesis. Hold it at path-dependence and the double cover, not at "the minus sign is bad."

The genuinely interesting break is `erasePerson`. Everything else in that data layer is information-preserving — supersession retains, resolution retains, the audit trail retains. GDPR erasure is the one operation that irreversibly destroys state. In the analogy it isn't a rotation at all; it's the measurement, the non-unitary step. And it's telling that the implementation is visibly uncomfortable about it: persisting `blobsPendingDeletion`, reporting `orphanedBlobUrls`, redacting rather than dropping the proposal history. It can't make the operation reversible, so it settles for making it accountable. That's the one place the name stops describing the system — which is probably the right place for a naming metaphor to break.

# Get API Docs via chub

When you need documentation for a library or API, fetch it with the `chub` CLI
rather than guessing from training data. This gives you the current, correct API.

## Step 1 — Find the right doc ID

```bash
chub search "<library name>" --json
```

Pick the best-matching `id` from the results (e.g. `openai/chat`, `anthropic/sdk`,
`stripe/api`). If nothing matches, try a broader term.

## Step 2 — Fetch the docs

```bash
chub get <id> --lang py    # or --lang js, --lang ts
```

Omit `--lang` if the doc has only one language variant — it will be auto-selected.

## Step 3 — Use the docs

Read the fetched content and use it to write accurate code or answer the question.
Do not rely on memorized API shapes — use what the docs say.

## Step 4 — Annotate what you learned

After completing the task, if you discovered something not in the doc — a gotcha,
workaround, version quirk, or project-specific detail — save it so future sessions
start smarter:

```bash
chub annotate <id> "Webhook verification requires raw body — do not parse before verifying"
```

Annotations are local, persist across sessions, and appear automatically on future
`chub get` calls. Keep notes concise and actionable. Don't repeat what's already in
the doc.

## Step 5 — Give feedback

Rate the doc so authors can improve it. Ask the user before sending.

```bash
chub feedback <id> up                        # doc worked well
chub feedback <id> down --label outdated     # doc needs updating
```

Available labels: `outdated`, `inaccurate`, `incomplete`, `wrong-examples`,
`wrong-version`, `poorly-structured`, `accurate`, `well-structured`, `helpful`,
`good-examples`.

## Quick reference

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| List everything | `chub search` |
| Find a doc | `chub search "stripe"` |
| Exact id detail | `chub search stripe/api` |
| Fetch Python docs | `chub get stripe/api --lang py` |
| Fetch JS docs | `chub get openai/chat --lang js` |
| Save to file | `chub get anthropic/sdk --lang py -o docs.md` |
| Fetch multiple | `chub get openai/chat stripe/api --lang py` |
| Save a note | `chub annotate stripe/api "needs raw body"` |
| List notes | `chub annotate --list` |
| Rate a doc | `chub feedback stripe/api up` |

## Notes

- `chub search` with no query lists everything available
- IDs are `<author>/<name>` — confirm the ID from search before fetching
- If multiple languages exist and you don't pass `--lang`, chub will tell you which are available

# GitHub App Permissions and Token Requirements for Self-Hosted Renovate

## Required Permissions

When creating a self-hosted GitHub App for Renovate, these permissions are mandatory:

| Permission | Scope |
|-----------|-------|
| Checks | `read` + `write` |
| Commit statuses | `read` + `write` |
| Contents | `read` + `write` |
| Issues | `read` + `write` |
| Pull requests | `read` + `write` |
| Workflows | `read` + `write` |
| Administration | `read` |
| Dependabot alerts | `read` |
| Members | `read` |
| Metadata | `read` |

## Installation Token Details

**Token Type**: You must use "a [GitHub App Installation token](https://docs.github.com/en/developers/apps/building-github-apps/authenticating-with-github-apps#authenticating-as-an-installation)" rather than a standard PAT.

**Token Lifespan**: Installation tokens "expire after 1 hour and need to be regenerated regularly."

**Token Format**: Tokens starting with `ghs_` don't require prefixes. However, tokens from GitHub Enterprise Server versions before 3.2 must be prefixed with `x-access-token:`.

## Configuration Methods

Supply the token through any of these approaches:
- `token` parameter in `config.js`
- `RENOVATE_TOKEN` environment variable
- CLI `--token=` parameter

Note: The documentation does not mention a `GITHUB_COM_TOKEN` environment variable specifically for this configuration.

# Current Recommended Usage of renovatebot/github-action

## Key Inputs

The action accepts several important inputs:

- **token**: A Personal Access Token (classic) with `repo` scope for public and private repositories
- **configurationFile**: JavaScript or JSON configuration file for global Renovate settings
- **renovate-version**: Specifies which Renovate version to use (defaults to a pinch version)
- **env-regex**: Pattern matching which environment variables pass to the container
- **docker-*** options**: For customizing Docker container behavior (user, volumes, socket mounting, etc.)

## Using a GitHub App Token

Rather than a personal access token tied to an individual, you can implement a GitHub App for better permission control. The recommended approach uses the `actions/create-github-app-token` action:

```yaml
- name: Get token
  id: get_token
  uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v1
  with:
    private-key: ${{ secrets.private_key }}
    app-id: ${{ secrets.app_id }}
    owner: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
    repositories: 'repo1,repo2'
```

Then pass this token to the Renovate action as `token: '${{ steps.get_token.outputs.token }}'`.

## Complete Example Workflow

```yaml
name: Renovate
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0/15 * * * *'
jobs:
  renovate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v6.1.0
      - name: Self-hosted Renovate
        uses: renovatebot/github-action@v46.1.21
        with:
          configurationFile: example/renovate-config.js
          token: ${{ secrets.RENOVATE_TOKEN }}
```

This basic workflow runs every 15 minutes and requires the `RENOVATE_TOKEN` secret to be configured in your repository settings.

# Renovate's Bun Support

**File Matching:**
Renovate automatically detects bun projects by matching `"/(^|/)bun\.lockb?$/"` and `"/(^|/)package\.json$/"`. This means it recognizes both `bun.lock` and `bun.lockb` files.

**Lock File Maintenance:**
Yes, the manager supports lock file maintenance for both `bun.lockb` and `bun.lock`. The documentation notes that `"Lock file maintenance is delegated to the underlying package manager, which Renovate runs as an external command."` This indicates Renovate invokes bun directly to update lock files.

**Datasources:**
The manager supports extracting dependencies from npm and GitHub tags datasources.

**Important Caveat:**
When a `package.json` is found as part of bun results, it gets excluded from npm manager processing—*unless* an npm/pnpm/Yarn lock file is also present. This prevents duplicate processing.

**Not Addressed:**
The documentation provided doesn't mention workspace support, bun binary availability requirements, or other potential caveats beyond the package.json exclusion behavior noted above.

name: Renovate

# Self-hosted replacement for the Mend Cloud Runner that drives hasToggle.dev.
# The bot identity is a GitHub App owned by the org (see docs/renovate.md);
# nothing here depends on a human's personal access token.

on:
  schedule:
    # Every four hours. This only controls how often Renovate wakes up and
    # looks — what it is allowed to open is decided by renovate.json.
    - cron: "0 */4 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      logLevel:
        description: Log level
        type: choice
        default: info
        options:
          - debug
          - info
          - warn
      dryRun:
        description: Dry run — resolve everything, write nothing
        type: boolean
        default: false

# Two overlapping runs duplicate branch work and can race each other's
# automerge step. Queue rather than cancel so a scheduled tick is never lost.
concurrency:
  group: renovate
  cancel-in-progress: false

# The job's own GITHUB_TOKEN does nothing here — every write goes through the
# App installation token minted below.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  renovate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Mint an App installation token
        id: app-token
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v3
        with:
          app-id: ${{ secrets.RENOVATE_APP_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.RENOVATE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          owner: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
          repositories: ${{ github.event.repository.name }}

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          # Renovate clones the repo itself with the App token; the checkout is
          # only here to give the action a workspace. Leaving the Actions
          # credentials behind in .git/config would serve no purpose.
          persist-credentials: false

      # Setting the env var only when the input is true keeps RENOVATE_DRY_RUN
      # absent on normal runs — an empty string is not a valid dryRun value.
      - name: Enable dry run
        if: ${{ inputs.dryRun }}
        run: echo "RENOVATE_DRY_RUN=full" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Renovate
        uses: renovatebot/github-action@v46.2.0
        with:
          token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
          # Floats within the major so patches arrive without a config bump;
          # Renovate keeps the `uses:` pin above current by itself.
          renovate-version: 44
        env:
          # Global (self-hosted) config lives here rather than in a config file
          # so there is one place to read. The action forwards any RENOVATE_*
          # and LOG_LEVEL vars into the container.
          RENOVATE_PLATFORM: github
          RENOVATE_REPOSITORIES: ${{ github.repository }}
          # renovate.json is already committed, so the onboarding-PR flow is
          # dead weight — and requiring config means a run against a repo
          # without one fails loudly instead of silently doing nothing.
          RENOVATE_ONBOARDING: "false"
          RENOVATE_REQUIRE_CONFIG: required
          LOG_LEVEL: ${{ inputs.logLevel || 'info' }}

# Renovate (self-hosted)

`hasToggle.dev` is kept current by the Mend-hosted Renovate Cloud Runner. This
repo is not installed on that app, so it runs its own Renovate from
`.github/workflows/renovate.yml`, authenticated as an org-owned GitHub App.

Dependency policy itself lives in `renovate.json` at the repo root and is
unchanged from the upstream template. This document only covers the runner.

## Why a GitHub App rather than a PAT

- The token is a short-lived installation token (1 hour), minted per run, not a
  long-lived secret tied to a person's account.
- Pull requests are authored by the app, not by whoever's PAT it is, so
  `git log` and the PR list stay honest about what is automation.
- The app has its own API rate limit rather than sharing a human's.
- **Pull requests opened with an App token trigger other workflows.** Ones
  opened with the job's built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not — CI would never run on
  a Renovate PR, and with `automerge: true` that means merging unverified.

## One-time setup

### 1. Create the App

Requires org-owner rights on `hasToggle`. The permission list is long and
getting one wrong fails at run time rather than at setup, so use the manifest
form generated at `.context/renovate-app-manifest.html` — open it in a browser
and it posts a pre-filled app definition to GitHub. Otherwise, create it by hand
at **Organization settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App**
with exactly these permissions ([source](https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/platform/github/)):

| Permission                  | Access       |
| --------------------------- | ------------ |
| Administration              | Read         |
| Checks                      | Read & write |
| Commit statuses             | Read & write |
| Contents                    | Read & write |
| Dependabot alerts           | Read         |
| Issues                      | Read & write |
| Members (organization)      | Read         |
| Metadata                    | Read         |
| Pull requests               | Read & write |
| Workflows                   | Read & write |

Subscribe to no events — this runner polls on a schedule and needs no webhook.
`Workflows: write` is what lets Renovate bump action versions inside
`.github/workflows/`; without it those updates fail while everything else
succeeds, which is a confusing way to find out.

### 2. Generate a private key and note the App ID

On the app's settings page: **Generate a private key** (downloads a `.pem`) and
copy the numeric **App ID** from the top of the page.

### 3. Install the App on this repo
